utterance: Good morning Graham, I'm the doctor. I can see you're not looking well at all, so let me ask you a few quick questions. Tell me about this indigestion — where exactly do you feel it, and what does it feel like? Is it pressure, squeezing, burning? Does it spread anywhere — to your arm, jaw, or back? And how bad is it out of 10?
reply: It's right in the middle, behind the breastbone, bit up into the throat. It's more heavy than sore, and now you mention it, my jaw's a bit achy and left arm feels heavy. Not my back. It started about seven this morning, came on over a few minutes. Maybe a six out of 10.

awards.label: Whether the discomfort spreads or travels anywhere (arms, jaw, neck, back)

utterance: Thanks, Graham. That description — heavy pressure behind the breastbone spreading to the jaw and left arm — is exactly the kind of pain I take very seriously, because it can be a sign of the heart not getting enough blood. I'm going to check you over right now and get a heart tracing (ECG) done immediately. Any breathlessness, nausea or vomiting, dizziness or palpitations with it? And is the heaviness constant since 7am, or does it come and go?
reply: A bit short of breath, feel a bit sick but haven't vomited, bit light-headed getting out of the car but didn't pass out. Heaviness's been constant since 7am.

awards.label: Red flag: Dizziness, light-headedness or fainting

result: Sinus bradycardia 54/min. ST elevation 2–3 mm in II, III and aVF. Reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. No LBBB.

awards.label: Call an ambulance (000) immediately for STEMI transfer

utterance: Graham, I need to be straight with you: the heart tracing shows you are having a heart attack — a blockage in one of the heart's arteries. This is treatable, but time is critical. I've called the ambulance, and I'm giving you aspirin now to chew — it thins the blood and helps stop the clot growing. The hospital will open the blocked artery, usually with a balloon procedure. Please stay sitting still and let the nurses know if the pain gets worse or you feel faint.
reply: I'm having a heart attack. I didn't think it was that bad. What happens next?

utterance: Here's what happens next, Graham. The ambulance will take you to the hospital where the heart team is being alerted. They'll do a procedure called an angioplasty — a thin tube through your wrist or groin to open the blocked artery, usually with a small balloon and a stent (a tiny tube that keeps the artery open). That's the best treatment and it works best the sooner it's done, which is why we're moving fast. While we wait, I'll just have a quick listen to your chest and heart. Try to stay calm and still — sitting upright is best.
reply: I didn't think it was that bad. I'll do what you say.

finding: Heart sounds dual, soft S4. No murmur. No rub.

utterance: Chest and heart sound okay apart from the heart strain I expected. A couple of quick safety questions before the ambulance arrives: do you have any history of stomach ulcers or bleeding problems, and are you taking any blood thinners besides the aspirin I just gave you? And has your doctor ever mentioned heart trouble, angina or a family history of heart attacks?
reply: No bleeding problems, no blood thinners besides the aspirin. Never had heart trouble or angina. Dad had a heart attack at fifty-five, he died from it.

awards.label: Previous heart problems, angina, stents or heart operations
Family history of heart disease at a young age

utterance: Graham, the ambulance is on its way and the hospital heart team will be ready for you. To recap what I've done: the heart tracing showed a blockage causing a heart attack, I've given you a blood-thinning dose of aspirin, and the hospital will open the artery with a stent. I'm deliberately not giving you the angina spray because your blood pressure is a bit low and it could drop it further — the paramedics will manage your pain safely. While we wait: stay sitting upright and still, and tell me or the paramedics straight away if the pain gets worse, you feel faint, sweaty or breathless. One more thing that matters once you're through this: quitting smoking is the single biggest thing you can do to protect your heart going forward — we'll support you with that after you've recovered. You did the right thing coming in this morning; your wife saved your life.
reply: Sweating like anything, thought it was just hot. Twenty a day since I was a teenager, been meaning to quit.

awards.label: Red flag: Sweating or clamminess with the pain

utterance: That sweating is part of the heart attack, not the heat — the paramedics will keep a close eye on your heart rate and blood pressure, which is why staying with them matters. You're in the best possible place for this, Graham. The next few hours are about getting that artery open quickly, and your strong reaction to the aspirin is already working in your favour. We'll talk about quitting properly once you're out of hospital — there are treatments that make it much easier. I'll stay with you until the ambulance arrives.
reply: I didn't think it was that bad. I'll do what you say.
